answer: Over-sampling helps with class imbalance by <cite id="957f9a59-1">balancing the number of samples between classes by adding an instance copy of an underrepresented class or by generating artificial samples</cite>. In practice, this gives the minority class more representation during training; for example, <cite id="00b116d9-2">random over-sampling can be used to repeat some samples and balance the number of samples between the dataset</cite>. Common instance-level re-sampling strategies include <cite id="00b116d9-4">RandomOverSampler, which over-samples the minority class(es) by picking samples at random with replacement</cite>; <cite id="00b116d9-0">SMOTE, which generates new samples by interpolation</cite>; <cite id="00b116d9-5">ADASYN, which is similar to SMOTE but generates different numbers of samples depending on the local distribution of the class to be oversampled</cite>; <cite id="00b116d9-6">BorderlineSMOTE, which detects borderline samples and uses them to generate new synthetic samples</cite>; and <cite id="00b116d9-8">SVMSMOTE, which uses an SVM to detect the samples used for generating new synthetic samples</cite>. In short, over-sampling addresses imbalance by increasing minority-class presence, either through duplication or targeted synthetic-instance generation.<cite id="957f9a59-1,00b116d9-0"> </cite>

In grid-based 3D object detection, <cite id="9151bf8a-2">grid-based methods primarily utilize voxel or pillar representations.</cite> In <cite id="5473d138-4">voxel-based detection, the point cloud is divided into equally spaced 3D voxels</cite> and each voxel’s points are transformed into <cite id="5473d138-4">a unified feature</cite>, while recent comparisons note that voxel detectors <cite id="9151bf8a-2">deploy 3D</cite> convolutions on that 3D grid. In pillar-based methods such as PointPillars, points are organized into <cite id="8d8cc641-4,8d8cc641-5">vertical columns (pillars)</cite>; this representation is used to <cite id="8d8cc641-7">convert 3D point clouds into 2D pseudo-images, which can then be processed using standard CNNs</cite>, or more specifically <cite id="8aa55b4b-1">processed using lightweight 2D convolutional</cite> backbones in BEV. BEV is also widely used as an intermediate grid because <cite id="5473d138-2">voxelized features are then projected to a birds-eye view (BEV) representation that is compatible with standard 2D convolutions.</cite> Another common grid is range view: recent work says LiDAR 3D detectors use <cite id="b660150c-0">bird's-eye view (BEV) or range view (RV) as their primary basis</cite>, and RangeDet argues that <cite id="b660150c-2">Range View provides a compact 2D image</cite> for detection. Finally, some systems combine grids instead of choosing one: MVF aims to <cite id="8aa55b4b-5">synergize the birds-eye view and the perspective view</cite>, showing that multi-view fusion uses multiple grid representations to capture complementary information.

Pseudo-labels improve object localization mainly by using the predicted boxes from a pre-trained “teacher” detector as the annotations of unlabeled images to train the “student”, which leverages unlabeled images to improve the supervised object detector. In practice, localization gets better when methods account for box quality, because certainty-aware pseudo labels tailored for object detection can effectively estimate the classification and localization quality, and newer approaches explicitly remove misleading instances in regression pseudo-labels by considering relative uncertainty estimation from the Teacher and Student predictions. Likewise, methods such as RUPL report gains by model[ing] bounding box localization quality via uncertainty and remov[ing] misplaced pseudo-labels for regression. So, pseudo-labels help localization not just by adding more training boxes, but by adding more reliable box-regression supervision on unlabeled data.

The accelerator theory says firms choose a <cite id="P1,S1">desired capital stock that is proportional to output or sales</cite>, so <cite id="P1,S2">net investment rises when output is growing because firms need more capital to produce the higher level of demand</cite>. In simple form, <cite id="S2">investment depends on the change in output, not just its level</cite>, which means <cite id="P5,S4">faster GDP growth boosts capital spending, while slower growth—or recession—can cause investment to fall sharply even if output remains relatively high</cite>. At the same time, <cite id="S8,P2">the accelerator theory gives a smaller direct role to interest rates than neoclassical models</cite>, and <cite id="S9,P6,S5">its predictions weaken when firms have excess capacity, face high uncertainty, or are financially constrained</cite>.

Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) for THC analysis are typically synthesized by <cite id="S2">polymerizing monomers around a template molecule such as Δ9‑tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), then removing the template to leave recognition cavities that can selectively rebind THC</cite>. Two common routes are:

- <cite id="S2,S6">electropolymerized MIP films formed directly on electrode surfaces for sensing</cite>
- <cite id="S3">bulk polymerization using functional monomers such as methacrylic acid and crosslinkers such as ethylene glycol dimethacrylate, followed by grinding and washing to extract the template</cite>

For controlled substances, <cite id="S5">dummy-template imprinting is often used to avoid template bleeding, employing a structurally related analogue that still creates sites able to recognize THC or its metabolites</cite>.

Applications for selective detection include:

1. **Electrochemical THC sensors**  
   <cite id="S2">Screen-printed electrochemical sensors have been modified with electropolymerized THC-imprinted films</cite>, and <cite id="S6">binding is read out through voltammetric or impedance changes</cite>. These systems act as synthetic recognition layers for selective THC detection.

2. **Selective sample preparation before instrumental analysis**  
   <cite id="S3">Bulk cannabinoid MIPs have been incorporated into solid-phase extraction cartridges for selective extraction from biological samples</cite>.  
   In particular, <cite id="S4">molecularly imprinted solid-phase extraction (MISPE) has been reported for the THC metabolite 11-nor-9-carboxy-Δ9-THC (THC-COOH), selectively retaining it from urine before chromatographic analysis</cite>.

3. **Use in complex forensic/biological matrices**  
   <cite id="S7">Cannabinoid MIPs have been applied both as sample-preparation sorbents and as transducer-coupled recognition layers, improving selectivity in saliva, urine, and seized materials</cite>.

Selectivity is usually demonstrated by challenging the MIP with related compounds; <cite id="S8">cannabinoid MIPs are commonly tested against cannabidiol (CBD), cannabinol (CBN), and endogenous interferents to confirm preferential rebinding of the target</cite>.

In short: <cite id="S1">MIPs are antibody-like synthetic receptors for cannabinoids</cite> that are made by template-guided polymerization and then used either <cite id="S7">as selective extraction sorbents</cite> or <cite id="S2,S6">as electrochemical sensing layers</cite> for THC and metabolites such as <cite id="S4">THC-COOH</cite>.

Organic solvent additives affect vaterite mainly by changing both the <cite id="6e6a56b0-0">interaction of additives with Ca2+, the provision of active nucleation sites, and their bonding to preferential crystal surfaces, thereby preventing or modifying normal crystal growth</cite>. In practice, this means solvents/additives can alter the rate at which nuclei appear, which polymorph survives, how particles grow, and whether vaterite remains metastable or transforms.

For nucleation and precipitation kinetics, <cite id="9cf42e96-4,660411cd-4">the presence of an organic additive influenced the precipitation rate</cite>. More generally, additives can <cite id="18b70998-0">template the nucleation, growth and alignment of CaCO3</cite>. So organic solvents do not just passively dilute the medium; they shift the early-stage nucleation pathway and the subsequent crystallization trajectory.

For growth and morphology, solvent additives change how fast specific faces grow and therefore the final particle form. The solvent study reports that <cite id="9cf42e96-4">organic additives influenced ... the morphology</cite>, while the broader review states that additives <cite id="6e6a56b0-0">bond to a preferential surface by preventing or modifying growth</cite>. In addition, <cite id="660411cd-5">vaterite recrystallization to calcite and particle growth have been forcibly suppressed using organic solvents as additives</cite>, indicating that solvents can limit coarsening and help preserve smaller or less-transformed vaterite particles.

For phase stability, the overall baseline is that <cite id="6e6a56b0-3">vaterite [is] a metastable form of calcium carbonate</cite> and that <cite id="18b70998-3">the transformation of vaterite to calcite is believed to be based on a mechanism of dissolution of the metastable vaterite and growth of the stable calcite</cite>. Organic solvents can modify this transformation, but the effect depends on the solvent and synthesis route. In one direct precipitation study, <cite id="6e6a56b0-1,660411cd-0">the presence of all added organic solvents reduced the vaterite concentration in the produced CaCO3 both at the end of the reaction and after incubation</cite>, meaning lower vaterite retention under those conditions. Yet other reports show the opposite trend under different systems: <cite id="660411cd-2">methanol, isopropanol, and dimethyl sulfoxide inhibited the transformation of vaterite into calcite by increasing the saturation of the solution</cite>, and <cite id="18b70998-4">additives ... could prevent the transformation from vaterite to calcite</cite>. Also, solvent-specific interactions matter: <cite id="660411cd-1">DMSO molecules interacted with vaterite particles the most strongly, while the interaction of isopropanol with this polymorph was the weakest</cite>.

So, in summary: organic solvent additives can <cite id="18b70998-0,6e6a56b0-0">redirect nucleation and surface-selective growth</cite>, <cite id="9cf42e96-4,660411cd-5">change precipitation rate and suppress particle growth/recrystallization</cite>, <cite id="9cf42e96-4">alter morphology</cite>, and <cite id="6e6a56b0-1,660411cd-2,18b70998-4">either destabilize or stabilize vaterite depending on the solvent, its interaction strength, and the synthesis conditions</cite>.

The key effect of FeO interacting with SiO₂ is that it tends to form <cite id="d09e03bb-5">fayalite (2FeO·SiO₂)</cite> and related iron silicate melts/phases, and these are often comparatively low-melting or eutectic-forming. <cite id="a7d791c5-2">Iron and silicon are enriched in slag due to the adherence of low-melting-point ferro-silicate</cite>, and <cite id="a7d791c5-4">reaction of siderite/iron-bearing species with silicates can generate low-melting-point eutectics, resulting in higher slagging propensity</cite>.

That influences deposits in three main ways:

1. **Earlier melt formation / easier sticking**  
   Because Fe-bearing material plus silica can produce low-melting iron silicates, <cite id="a7d791c5-5">Fe-containing minerals lower the melting temperature of the deposited surface</cite>. A lower-melting surface becomes sticky sooner, so incoming particles are captured more readily and deposits grow faster.

2. **Lower viscosity and greater spreading/wetting in many compositions**  
   In FeO–SiO₂-bearing slags, <cite id="d09e03bb-3">increasing FeO/SiO₂ ratio decreased viscosity</cite>, and similarly <cite id="d09e03bb-4">slag viscosity decreases as Fe/SiO₂ increases from 0.8 to 1.2</cite>. Lower-viscosity melts can spread over surfaces, infiltrate pores, and act as a binder between ash/mineral particles, often making deposits denser and more tenacious.  
   There is, however, compositional nuance: <cite id="d09e03bb-0">a local viscosity maximum occurs around the fayalite composition in FeO–SiO₂ melts</cite>, so the exact deposit behavior depends on the FeO/SiO₂ ratio rather than FeO simply always lowering viscosity.

3. **Change in deposit composition and structure**  
   When silica-rich ash mixes with iron-bearing material, <cite id="d09e03bb-1">SiO₂, Al₂O₃, and other minerals mixed into iron ore pellet powder prompted the formation of silicates</cite>. This means FeO–SiO₂ interaction shifts deposits toward iron-silicate-rich matrices, which commonly bind other solids together and promote slag-like, consolidated deposits rather than loose particulate layers.

So, in short: **FeO + SiO₂ promotes iron-silicate formation, often lowers the melting temperature, frequently lowers viscosity, and therefore increases deposit stickiness, growth, densification, and slagging tendency**—though the precise characteristics depend strongly on the FeO/SiO₂ ratio and surrounding oxides.

In high-entropy alloys, these alloying elements mainly affect oxidation resistance by changing <cite id="2e8236bb-1,2e8236bb-3">which oxides form and whether the oxide scale is continuous and protective</cite>.

- **Aluminum (Al): generally improves oxidation resistance.**  
  <cite id="2e8236bb-1">Increased Al content has been shown to increase oxidation resistance by promoting formation of a continuous Al₂O₃ film.</cite>  
  <cite id="2e8236bb-3">The oxidation resistance of HEAs is improved with the addition of Al because of the formation of Al₂O₃.</cite>  
  In some refractory HEAs, Al-containing compositions also form <cite id="97e124e0-6">relatively thin oxide scales due to dense CrTaO₄ scales</cite>, and Al/Si alloying can <cite id="97e124e0-0,4710e217-0">enhance oxidation resistance by improving oxide-layer anti-spallation</cite>.  
  **Net effect:** Al tends to favor dense, adherent, slow-growing protective scales, especially alumina.

- **Titanium (Ti): often worsens oxidation resistance when TiO₂ dominates the scale.**  
  <cite id="97e124e0-5">Adding Ti degrades oxidation resistance due to the formation of less protective TiO₂ and Fe₃O₄.</cite>  
  In refractory HEAs, oxidation commonly produces <cite id="97e124e0-2">multi-layered oxide scales of titania (TiO₂), alumina (Al₂O₃), and chromia</cite>; if Ti oxidizes preferentially, the resulting TiO₂-rich outer layer is usually less protective than continuous alumina or chromia.  
  **Net effect:** Ti has strong oxygen affinity and promotes TiO₂ formation, but TiO₂ is often more porous/less protective, so excessive Ti can reduce oxidation resistance unless balanced by Al/Cr.

- **Molybdenum (Mo): usually has a mixed-to-negative effect on oxidation resistance at high temperature.**  
  The literature you retrieved points to oxidation-resistant RHEAs forming <cite id="97e124e0-2">multi-layered oxide scales</cite>, but Mo is generally problematic in high-temperature oxidation because Mo-containing alloys need improvement for service at high temperature: <cite id="2e8236bb-8">the poor oxidation resistance of molybdenum alloys greatly limits their application in high-temperature environments</cite>.  
  In Mo-containing refractory systems, better behavior is often achieved only when other elements stabilize the scale; for example, <cite id="4710e217-2">significant improvements in high-temperature oxidation behavior of Mo-based alloys have been achieved due to macroalloying with Ti</cite>.  
  **Net effect:** Mo by itself does not usually form the most protective oxide scale; in HEAs it often contributes to complex, multi-layer oxide formation and typically requires Al/Cr/Si or other alloying strategies to obtain good oxidation resistance.

**Overall trend:**  
<cite id="2e8236bb-1,97e124e0-2,97e124e0-5">Al is the most beneficial of the three because it promotes continuous protective alumina; Ti often promotes less-protective TiO₂-rich scales; and Mo tends to complicate oxidation behavior and is usually not sufficient for protection unless combined with scale-forming elements such as Al or Cr.</cite>

1. **Classical handcrafted-feature pipelines**  
   These typically use preprocessing such as <cite id="S9">binarization, thinning, slant correction, and size normalization</cite>, followed by features like <cite id="S7">histogram of oriented gradients (HOG), gradient local auto-correlation, and directional gradient features</cite> or <cite id="S5">structural and topological features—such as endpoints, junctions, loops, and headline (shirorekha) information</cite>. In end-milling of composites, surface damage and quality are driven mainly by how machining parameters change <cite id="c63a246d-0">cutting forces, temperatures, surface roughness, and damage defects</cite>.

- **Feed rate is often the strongest lever on surface quality.** Reviews report that <cite id="180da51e-1">surface roughness is less dependent on the cutting speed as compared to the feed rate and the fiber winding angle</cite>, and one milling study recommended <cite id="180da51e-2">low cutting speed and high feed rate (200 m/min and 0.15 mm/tooth) ... Feed rate was the most significant</cite> for surface integrity/roughness. In practice, higher feed tends to increase instantaneous chip load and force, which promotes damage such as tearing, pull-out, and rougher surfaces.

- **Cutting speed has a mixed but important effect.** Some studies found that raising speed can help: <cite id="081a683c-1">tool wear decreased with increasing cutting speed under a consistent feed per tooth, which further led to a reduction in the cutting force, burr area</cite>. But other work found the opposite for CFRP, where <cite id="180da51e-8">milling CFRP with Vc = 132 m/min resulted in increasing of tool wear by 15% and increasing of surface roughness by 10% when compared with Vc = 94 m/min</cite>. So the effect of speed is material/system dependent: if higher speed stabilizes cutting and reduces force, quality improves; if it accelerates wear or thermal damage, quality worsens.

- **Fiber orientation/machining direction strongly affects damage formation.** In CF/PEEK milling, <cite id="c63a246d-0">the cutting force, temperature, and surface quality were optimal at a fiber direction of 0° and were least favorable at 90° under identical machining conditions</cite>. A separate study also reported that <cite id="081a683c-0">surface roughness showed a reciprocal decrease with machining</cite> direction effects tied to feed force and wear, and another snippet notes <cite id="081a683c-7">the surface roughness increased as the fiber orientation</cite> changed unfavorably. This is because fiber angle changes whether fibers are cut cleanly or tend to bend, fracture, debond, or pull out.

- **Tool wear directly degrades surface finish.** One study observed <cite id="081a683c-0">a strong correlation ... between feed force and tool wear</cite>, while another found that reducing wear via cutting-speed choice also reduced <cite id="081a683c-1">cutting force, burr area</cite>. As the edge dulls, forces rise and the machined surface shows more matrix smearing, uncut fibers, fuzzing, burrs, and delamination-like edge damage.

- **Typical surface damage modes are brittle fracture, pull-out, and debonding.** For CF/PEEK, <cite id="c63a246d-0">brittle fracture is the primary material removal mechanism, with damage characteristics such as fiber fracture, fiber pullout, and fiber/matrix debonding</cite>. Machining parameters that raise force/temperature generally intensify these defects.

- **Parameter optimization can significantly improve quality.** The same CF/PEEK study found that laser assistance <cite id="c63a246d-0">significantly reduces surface defects and improves surface roughness</cite>, with an <cite id="c63a246d-0">optimal parameter combination ... 0° fiber orientation, 400 W laser power, and a spindle speed of 4000 rpm</cite>. More generally, end-milling quality improves when parameters are chosen to minimize force and wear for the specific composite, tool, and fiber orientation.

**Bottom line:** surface quality in composite end-milling is usually most sensitive to **feed rate** and **fiber orientation**, while **cutting speed** has a conditional effect through force, wear, and heat. Poor parameter choices increase **roughness, burrs, fiber pull-out, fracture, and fiber/matrix debonding**; good choices minimize force and tool wear and produce cleaner fiber cutting.

### Core damage mechanisms

UV radiation injures cells through both <cite id="0241598a-2">direct interactions of DNA with UV photons</cite> and <cite id="0241598a-2,95908ad6-1">indirect oxidative stress driven by reactive oxygen species (ROS)</cite>. The best-characterized direct DNA lesions are <cite id="3045ae4e-1,3045ae4e-7">cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and (6–4) pyrimidine-pyrimidone photoproducts</cite>, which distort DNA and are mutagenic. In parallel, <cite id="3045ae4e-0,95908ad6-5">UV-stimulated ROS cause oxidative DNA damage</cite>, and <cite id="95908ad6-1,95908ad6-6">long-term or chronic UV exposure promotes oxidative stress, inflammation, and increased mutation burden</cite>.

### How damage is translated into cell-fate decisions

Cells do not respond to all UV injury the same way: <cite id="95908ad6-0,265d3abb-4">after lower UV doses the stress response tends to favor DNA repair, whereas higher doses favor apoptosis</cite>. A key regulator of this switch is p53; <cite id="265d3abb-6,95908ad6-9">p53 contributes to nucleotide excision repair (NER), the main pathway that removes UV-induced DNA damage</cite>. When lesions persist or become too extensive, the damaged cell is pushed away from survival and toward programmed death.

### Apoptotic pathways activated by UV

Mechanistically, <cite id="3045ae4e-2">UV-induced apoptosis reflects a synergistic contribution from three major pathways: DNA damage, death-receptor signaling, and ROS</cite>. In epidermal keratinocytes, <cite id="8da699ee-1,8da699ee-8">UV activates both membrane death-receptor pathways and the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic pathway</cite>. The mitochondrial arm is supported by findings that <cite id="8da699ee-0">Bcl-2 overexpression potently inhibits UVR-induced apoptosis</cite> and that <cite id="8da699ee-2">p38 MAPK activation is required for Bax translocation to mitochondria, cytochrome c release, and apoptosis</cite>; execution of death also involves <cite id="8da699ee-6">caspase-mediated signaling in human keratinocytes</cite>.

### Biological consequence

This apoptotic response is fundamentally protective: <cite id="265d3abb-1,3045ae4e-4">UV-induced apoptosis removes DNA-damaged cells and thereby reduces the risk of malignant transformation</cite>. In short, UV light causes <cite id="3045ae4e-1,0241598a-2">direct photochemical DNA lesions</cite> and <cite id="3045ae4e-0,95908ad6-1">ROS-mediated oxidative injury</cite>; if repair is insufficient, <cite id="95908ad6-0,8da699ee-1">p53-linked stress responses, death-receptor signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction, MAPK/Bax/cytochrome c signaling, and caspase activation</cite> drive the cell into apoptosis.

## Strongest evidence: chronic migraine

The best-established analgesic indication is chronic migraine. Two large PREEMPT trials provided pivotal evidence: <cite id="9a2a491d-1">PREEMPT 1 and 2 were randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies with 1,384 patients across 122 sites</cite>. Their pooled analysis found that <cite id="9a2a491d-0">onabotulinumtoxinA is an effective prophylactic treatment for chronic migraine</cite>, and a Cochrane-based meta-analysis reported that <cite id="35dd2e7c-5">botulinum toxin reduced migraine frequency by about 2.0 migraine days per month versus placebo in chronic migraineurs</cite>. Review articles also summarize that <cite id="6abb9244-1">efficacy in chronic migraine was shown in two large industry-sponsored randomized controlled clinical trials</cite> and that <cite id="6abb9244-4">PREEMPT data showed a mean reduction of approximately 2 headache days over 4 weeks compared with placebo</cite>.

### Study designs used in chronic migraine
The core supporting designs were <cite id="9a2a491d-1">large multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials</cite>, followed by <cite id="35dd2e7c-5">systematic review/meta-analysis pooling trial data</cite>. This is the highest-quality clinical evidence represented in the retrieved sources.

For regenerated sunflower plants, the methods most commonly used to determine ploidy are:

1. <cite id="948b01c3-1">direct chromosome counting</cite>  
2. <cite id="af03e603-0">flow cytometric measurement of nuclear DNA content</cite>  
3. Indirect morphological/cytological screens such as <cite id="948b01c3-1">stomatal size</cite>, <cite id="948b01c3-1">chloroplast number of the guard cells</cite>, and sometimes broader <cite id="948b01c3-7">plant morphology, leaf shape/size, pollen size, guard cell size</cite>.

In practice, the main **direct** approach is <cite id="948b01c3-1">chromosome counting</cite>, while the main **indirect** approaches are <cite id="948b01c3-1">flow cytometry, stomatal size, chloroplast number of the guard cells</cite>.

### Direct vs. indirect approaches

- **Direct methods**
  - The classic direct method is <cite id="948b01c3-1">chromosome counting</cite>.
  - It is generally regarded as highly reliable because it measures the chromosomes themselves; likewise, a plant-breeding review notes that <cite id="d9675f4a-4">the most reliable methods to confirm the ploidy level in plants are to count the chromosomes or to measure the DNA in the cells</cite>.
  - Its drawback is labor and technical difficulty; a recent summary notes that <cite id="d9675f4a-8">determining plant ploidy level through chromosome counting at the metaphase stage using a microscope is widely practiced, this method requires highly ...</cite> specialized effort.

- **Indirect methods**
  - **Flow cytometry** is now the most widely favored indirect method because <cite id="af03e603-0">flow cytometric analysis has been an efficient and popular method to determine ploidy levels for higher plants, based on the precise measurement for DNA content</cite>.
  - A best-practices guideline states that <cite id="af03e603-5">FCM has almost completely replaced traditional methods for establishing ploidy</cite>, including traditional direct and indirect approaches.
  - Other indirect methods—especially useful for rapid screening—include <cite id="948b01c3-1">stomatal size</cite> and <cite id="948b01c3-1">chloroplast number of the guard cells</cite>. These traits tend to scale with ploidy; for example, one study reports that <cite id="d9675f4a-3">length and diameter of stomata and chloroplast number in stomata of guard cells increased with increased ploidy level</cite>.

### Bottom line

For regenerated sunflower plants, the standard workflow is usually:

- use <cite id="af03e603-0">flow cytometry</cite> for fast, high-throughput ploidy screening,
- confirm key plants by <cite id="948b01c3-1">chromosome counting</cite>,
- and optionally use <cite id="948b01c3-1">stomatal size</cite> or <cite id="948b01c3-1">chloroplast number of the guard cells</cite> as simple preliminary indicators.

So, **direct methods are more definitive but slower and more labor-intensive; indirect methods are faster and easier for screening, with flow cytometry generally giving the best combination of speed and accuracy.**

Exosomal components—especially <cite id="dDw5FPB8IEwJ">miRNAs</cite> and <cite id="dDw5FPB8IEwJ">proteins, lipids and nucleic acids</cite>—are useful fibrosis biomarkers because they combine <cite id="Rt77YwpNO6Y5">accessibility from body fluids</cite> with <cite id="o3sg5WtO7hHB">cargo that reflects the physiological or pathological state of the producer cells</cite>. In practice, that makes them attractive for monitoring fibrosis progression in several ways:

1. **They are noninvasive and repeatable.**  
   Conventional fibrosis assessment often depends on <cite id="Rt77YwpNO6Y5">invasive tissue biopsies</cite>, whereas exosomes/extracellular vesicles <cite id="o3sg5WtO7hHB">can be found in body fluids such as blood, urine, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and saliva</cite> and <cite id="o3sg5WtO7hHB">can be collected repeatedly with relatively little invasiveness</cite>. This is what makes them practical for longitudinal monitoring.

2. **Their cargo is relatively stable.**  
   Exosomes are considered good biomarkers because <cite id="dDw5FPB8IEwJ">they can be detected in almost all body fluids</cite> and <cite id="dDw5FPB8IEwJ">carry and preserve proteins, lipids and nucleic acids for disease diagnosis and prognostic prediction</cite>. In particular, <cite id="dDw5FPB8IEwJ">exosomal miRNAs maintain excellent stability</cite>, and exosomes <cite id="iJOdbiL0y4K_">protect miRNAs from degradation by surrounding ribonucleases</cite>. That stability improves analytic reliability.

3. **They track the biology driving fibrosis.**  
   Fibrosis progression is not just accompanied by exosomes; exosomes are involved in it. In organ fibrosis, <cite id="b4EJAS92G6hA">exosomes secreted by injured epithelial cells, vascular endothelial cells, and activated fibroblasts can all regulate fibroblast activation</cite>. Because their contents come from the cells orchestrating fibrosis, exosomal cargo can mirror ongoing disease activity rather than just static tissue damage.

4. **They can be organ-relevant.**  
   In kidney disease, for example, <cite id="jIuk-Zt2wyHK">urinary exosomes can be representative of renal tissue and accessible in a noninvasive way</cite>, which is why they are described as <cite id="jIuk-Zt2wyHK">ideal biomarkers in kidney disease</cite>. Similarly for liver disease, <cite id="Rw5_L3W70rAO">exosomes can be isolated from a wide variety of body fluids such as blood and urine</cite> and <cite id="Rw5_L3W70rAO">can be used as biomarkers to identify liver disease and estimate liver fibrosis and inflammation</cite>.

5. **Specific exosomal miRNAs already correlate with fibrosis progression.**  
   For hepatic fibrosis, <cite id="932c8899-0">exosomal miR-155 can act as a non-invasive biomarker for the diagnosis and progression of hepatic fibrosis</cite>. Also, <cite id="932c8899-5">exosomal miR-122 may serve as a useful non-invasive biomarker for liver fibrosis</cite>. For kidney fibrosis, <cite id="i0ZqWB9HvYPr">urinary exosomal miR-21 is a stable and potential indicator of kidney fibrosis progression</cite>.

**Bottom line:** exosomal biomarkers are reliable and practical for fibrosis monitoring because <cite id="dDw5FPB8IEwJ">their cargo is stable</cite>, <cite id="o3sg5WtO7hHB">reflects the diseased cell state</cite>, and <cite id="o3sg5WtO7hHB,Rt77YwpNO6Y5">can be repeatedly sampled from body fluids with much less invasiveness than biopsy</cite>. The most developed examples are exosomal miRNAs, which have shown utility in tracking progression in liver and kidney fibrosis.

In this literature, readability is usually treated as the ease or difficulty of understanding the text itself—that is, how demanding a passage is in terms of vocabulary, sentence structure, cohesion, and overall language complexity. Linguistic/experimental indicators, such as word frequency, syntactic complexity, cohesion, or researcher-created manipulations of passage difficulty. So, when readability is a moderator, researchers generally operationalize it as a text-difficulty variable and test whether the relation between some predictor (for example, decoding, vocabulary, or instruction) and inferential comprehension is stronger or weaker for texts with different readability levels.
